* How are the directions N, E, S, and W defined on the grid?

* Is it guaranteed that a solution always exists? What if F is too low?

* In my opinion, it's Hard, not Very Hard. I'd like to hear what everyone else thinks.

Thank you.

It's good that you've kept the old contribution https://www.codingame.com/contribute/view/13049762d2e2a917ec6104537787b521c9b6e8, as I'd still like to refer to the previous comments there.

Goal
* Please change "weighs between 1 to 1000" to "has a weight".

Cover picture
* Consider uploading a cover picture for the puzzle.

Cases
* Test 20: Please swap "249 0 1" and "125 0 1".

* The y-coordinates of some packages exceed [[l]]:
  • Tests 13, 17, 18, 19
  • Validators 17, 18, 19

* Please reduce the grid sizes to minimise empty areas:
  [edit: ignore this point]

* Minor point: if possible, please adjust the grid sizes or even rotate grids to improve balance:

  l < w: 7 tests and 9 validators
  l = w: 11 tests and 9 validators
  l > w: 3 tests and 3 validators (very few)

* Minor point: if possible, please design a few grids so that the layout is "more horizontal" (i.e. range of x-coordinates > range of y-coordinates; Test 7 and Validator 7 are very extreme examples) and a few other grids so that the layout is "more vertical" (i.e. range of y-coordinates > range of x-coordinates). I like some of the existing special designs, so please don't modify those (e.g. Tests/Validators 10, 11 and 12).

* Reordering and coverage: pending review.

Thanks.

I still need to reorder the new test cases I added (Test 16 might be the most difficult, so I may plan to move it to the end). Other than that, I’d really appreciate it if you could like my contribution or share any feedback you have! :)

> In my opinion, it's Hard, not Very Hard. I'd like to hear what everyone else thinks.

I haven't tried solving the puzzle myself, so I can't really judge the difficulty accurately.

A quick look at the author's solution shows the use of NumPy, bitmasking and lru_cache. If relatively advanced functions and substantial optimisation are genuinely required to solve the puzzle, then a Very Hard classification may be justified. Otherwise, Hard, as you suggested.

I noticed that some input grids contain large areas of irrelevant space. For example, in Test 16, the grid is 36 x 29, while the relevant region is only about 4 x 6. The author's solution spends a relatively long time on such cases. If the search space is restricted to the relevant area, the runtime will likely be reduced significantly.

####################

Separately, I think the ordering of the cases may still need adjustment. Using the author's solution runtime as a rough proxy for search-space complexity, the difficulty doesn't increase consistently from one case to the next.

I also still need to take a closer look at the current case coverage.

Given these outstanding questions, I think the author should consider switching the puzzle status back to WIP for now.

A few questions for @kozuechan:

1. How does your own solution compare? Does it rely on relatively advanced techniques or heavy optimisation?

2. What are your thoughts on the current ordering of the test cases?

3. What do you think of the current case coverage?

Thank you for your reply, @5DN1L.

I usually expect a Very Hard puzzle to take several days to solve, but I was able to get an implementation that passes all cases within a single day for this one.

> A quick look at the author's solution shows the use of NumPy, bitmasking and lru_cache.

NumPy and bitmasking are not necessary. My solution doesn't use either of them. As for lru_cache, it improves the time complexity at an order-of-magnitude level and is one of the core elements of this puzzle. That lru_cache can be rewritten into a bottom-up DP.

> Using the author's solution runtime as a rough proxy for search-space complexity, the difficulty doesn't increase consistently from one case to the next.

If it helps you review this puzzle, I don't mind sharing my solution code with you @5DN1L in a private message.

> 1. How does your own solution compare? Does it rely on relatively advanced techniques or heavy optimisation?

My solution relies mostly on algorithm-level techniques. I can definitely optimize it much further at the code level.

> 2. What are your thoughts on the current ordering of the test cases?
> 3. What do you think of the current case coverage?

I need to investigate further to answer these questions.

> If it helps you review this puzzle, I don't mind sharing my solution code with you @5DN1L in a private message.

Thanks for the offer. I'd appreciate that.
I have just sent you a private message on the forum.

Thanks for all the feedback! I've updated the puzzle to Hard difficulty and clarified the statement by specifying how directions are defined on the grid.

I think this puzzle has the potential to become a Very Hard problem, so I'm currently brainstorming ways to make it trickier. If anyone has any ideas or suggestions, I'd be more than happy to consider them.

Two minor points for @NicknamedTwice to follow up first:

Input
* Next k lines: Please add "three integers" after "contains".

Constraints
* (In response to @kozuechan's first comment) Please state explicitly that, for every test case, [[F]] is always sufficient so that a solution exists.

##################

I've run the solution of both @NicknamedTwice and @kozuechan, and observed the following:

* @kozuechan's solution is consistently slower, except for the first pair of cases. That said, it still runs within the time limit.

* The runtimes of both solutions generally correlate well: cases that take longer for one solution also tend to take longer for the other.

* If @kozuechan's runtime is used as the sole criterion for ordering the test cases, then Pairs 7, 8, 9, 12, 16, 17, 18, and 20 appear to be out of order.

* I don't know how @NicknamedTwice designed the current test set (well, I know some of them were designed by other CodinGamers), or whether certain cases were created to target specific scenarios, features, or objectives. If so, those considerations should also be taken into account when deciding on any reordering. Before discussing that further, I'd be interested in seeing a brief summary from @NicknamedTwice describing the intent behind or the scenario covered by each case pair. (For example, is it about the way how entities are distributed on the grid? Or is it about the magnitudes of grid size and other variables?)

* As @NicknamedTwice previously mentioned that they would prefer not to reorder cases every time new ones are added, I'd simply note that this should be revisited once the test set has been finalised.
